intro: “Der Dichter spricht” (The Poet Speaks) is No. 13, the last piece, of Kinderszenen, Op. 15, and follows “Kind im Einschlummern”. A G major hymn is interrupted by an unbarred recitative in the treble, then returns with a longer ending.

sections.label: C · Piano passage without barlines
sections.mNote: Little runs, grace notes and pauses in the treble.

sections.label: A′ · The hymn returns
sections.mNote: The last chords descend and slow into G major.

cues.title: Opening chords in G major
cues.text: Both hands begin with piano chords in G major, in common time. The inner voices move by step. The phrase swells under a hairpin and closes before the music begins again.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, plate 6016, p. 20, opening systems: common time, G major, piano and hairpins in chordal writing. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/f/fe/IMSLP03060-Schumann-Op015Brt6016.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Unbarred recitative
cues.text: The piano leaves the hymn. Short runs and grace notes move through the treble, pianissimo, and pause under fermatas. Schumann writes the passage without barlines, as an unbarred recitative in triplet groups (first edition, Breitkopf & Härtel, p. 20, third system).
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 20, third system: unbarred recitative, triplet groups, grace notes, pianissimo and fermatas.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the opening chords
cues.text: The opening chords return in G major. The ending is longer this time. The chords descend, the ritardando extends over the final bars and the bass reaches a low G, and the last chord is held under a fermata.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 20, final two systems: return of the opening, extended ritardando and final G-major chord.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The hymn breaks into descending lines
transitions.how: The G major hymn divides into separate descending lines. The bass moves beneath held upper notes. A ritardando and fermatas interrupt the regular four-beat bars, and each continuation follows a pause.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 20, second system: piano descending figures, ritardando and fermatas.

transitions.title: Fermata before the unbarred recitative
transitions.how: The descending bass reaches a fermata and stops. The right hand then plays small triplet figures marked pianissimo. From this point the passage has no barlines, and grace notes and chromatic turns take it up into the treble.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 20, beginning of the unbarred third system.

transitions.title: Return to the G major hymn
transitions.how: The free piano line descends through chromatic notes and slows with a ritardando. At the double bar the G major hymn returns, marked piano. Both hands go back to measured chords, and the four-beat bars begin again.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 20, end of the unbarred passage and start of the fourth system.

fields.label: Performers

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The sources do not say which printed edition Donald Betts played from. Schumann’s Kinderszenen exist in a pre-publication printing, the 1839 first edition and its revised second issue, and Clara Schumann’s later edition; the recording is not matched to any of them here.

composer.epithet: Composer and music critic, a bookseller’s son, whose piano music depicts lovers, masks and arguments.
facts: Friedrich Wieck, piano; Heinrich Dorn, composition
Co-founded the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik in 1834; edited it until 1844
Married Clara Wieck in 1840; eight children, seven surviving infancy
composer.background:
Robert Schumann grew up among books in Zwickau. His father August sold and published them, and encouraged his son’s music; Robert read Jean Paul’s novels while learning the piano. The novels contain twins, disguises, and conversations that wander from their subject and return to it unexpectedly. In Papillons, his early set of piano dances, Schumann took up the masked ball at the end of Jean Paul’s Flegeljahre.

He went to Leipzig to study law in 1828 and moved to Heidelberg the following year. In the end he persuaded his mother to let him pursue music. Friedrich Wieck undertook to train him as a pianist. Wieck’s young daughter Clara was already performing in public; Robert was the older pupil and had more ground to make up. By 1832 paralysis in his right hand had ended his hopes of becoming a virtuoso. He studied composition with Heinrich Dorn and turned to composing and writing.
